add_eyes.name: Piero di Marco Parenti
add_eyes.role: Florentine merchant and office-holder, son of Marco Parenti and Caterina Strozzi; in his forties and fifties during these years
add_eyes.side: Florence; republican patrician, increasingly hostile to Savonarola
add_eyes.where: Florence, in and around the palace and the councils
add_eyes.vantage_label: patrician chronicler from the friar's critics
add_eyes.authenticity: The Storia fiorentina survives in manuscript at the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence, and is being edited by Andrea Matucci (Olschki, 1994– ; vol. II, 1496–1502, appeared in 2005). It is written up year by year, close to the events, but it is a chronicle with reflection, not a day-book.
add_eyes.bio: Parenti wrote from the same streets as Landucci, but from the patrician benches and with growing hostility to the friar's party. He records the ordeal, the fall of San Marco and the execution as a political story about factions and the Signoria, not as a believer's grief. Set beside Landucci he gives the chapter both camps on Savonarola.

sources.title: Piero Parenti, Storia fiorentina, vol. II (1496–1502), ed. A. Matucci (Olschki, 2005)

add_eyes.name: Marin Sanudo the Younger
add_eyes.role: Venetian patrician and historian, about 30 in 1496; member of the Great Council, later a senator
add_eyes.side: Republic of Venice (rival of Florence, backer of Pisa)
add_eyes.where: Venice, copying the letters and dispatches that reached the Council
add_eyes.authenticity: The Diarii run from January 1496 to 1533 in 58 manuscript volumes (Biblioteca Marciana); printed in full as I diarii di Marin Sanudo, ed. R. Fulin, F. Stefani and others (Venice, 1879–1903). Much of each entry is copied letters from ambassadors, captains and merchants, so the day of an entry is often the day news arrived, not the day of the event.
add_eyes.bio: Sanudo wrote down nearly everything that reached Venice, day after day for thirty-seven years. Florence appears in his pages as a news story and an enemy: the friar's fall arrives as letters from merchants and agents, and the war over Pisa arrives as reports from Venetian paymasters in the field. He shows how the Florentine decade looked from a rival republic.

sources.title: Selection with English translation: Venice, Cità Excelentissima (Johns Hopkins, 2008), notice
A letter copied into the Diarii, vol. 1, coll. 300–301 (De Re Militari translation)

add_eyes.name: Isabella d'Este, Marchioness of Mantua
add_eyes.role: Marchioness of Mantua, aged 26–30; collector building her studiolo
add_eyes.where: The Gonzaga palace in Mantua, writing to agents in Florence
add_eyes.vantage_label: patron at a distance, working through agents
add_eyes.form: dated letters (her own, and those written to her)
add_eyes.authenticity: Her outgoing letter-books and the incoming letters survive in the Archivio Gonzaga, Archivio di Stato di Mantova; the Leonardo letters are catalogued and printed in the archive's own Leonardo publication and in F. Villata, Leonardo da Vinci: i documenti e le testimonianze (1999). Dates are from the letters.
add_eyes.bio: Leonardo had drawn her in charcoal at Mantua in the winter of 1499–1500 and promised a painted version that never came. For five years she pursued him through agents in Florence, and the replies she received are the only dated eyewitness reports of what was on his easel in 1501. She is a patron's and a woman's voice on the art, and her pursuit runs straight across the David's journey and the Anghiari commission.

sources.title: Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Leonardo e l'Archivio di Stato (catalogue of the letters)

add_eyes.name: Fra Pietro da Novellara
add_eyes.role: Carmelite friar, vicar-general of his order, acting as Isabella d'Este's agent in Florence in 1501
add_eyes.where: Florence, visiting Leonardo where he lodged with the Servites at Santissima Annunziata
add_eyes.authenticity: Two letters to Isabella d'Este, dated Florence 3 and 14 April 1501, in the Archivio Gonzaga, Archivio di Stato di Mantova; long known to Leonardo scholarship and printed in the standard document collections.
add_eyes.bio: Novellara called on Leonardo at Isabella's request and wrote down what he saw: a cartoon of the Virgin and St Anne, a small Madonna for a French royal secretary, two assistants making portraits, and a master who would rather do geometry than paint. His two letters give Leonardo the dated studio visit the chapter otherwise lacks.

sources.title: Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Leonardo e l'Archivio di Stato (letters of 3 and 14 April 1501)

add_entries.headline: The ordeal by fire collapses into argument
add_entries.digest: Parenti tells the ordeal as a contest of factions: the Franciscans' challenge, the Signoria's platform, and a long afternoon of disputes over vestments and the Host until rain and nightfall ended it with no one entering the fire. To him the outcome was a political defeat for the friar's party, whose followers went home shamed while their enemies took heart.
add_entries.source_note: Parenti, Storia fiorentina, ed. Matucci, vol. II (1496–1502), under April 1498; day of the ordeal is certain, the wording of his entry not checked here.

add_entries.headline: A chronicler of the other camp records the execution
add_entries.digest: Parenti records the degradation, hanging and burning of the three friars as the close of a political crisis rather than a martyrdom. Where Landucci grieved, Parenti's interest is in the trial, the papal commissioners and what the end of the friar's party meant for the government.
add_entries.source_note: Parenti, Storia fiorentina, vol. II, under May 1498 (ed. Matucci, 2005); content summarised from the chronicle's coverage, exact entry not checked here.

add_entries.place: Florence, the route from the Opera to the Piazza
add_entries.headline: Stones thrown at the giant by night
add_entries.digest: Parenti noted the moving of Michelangelo's marble giant towards the palace, and that young men threw stones at it by night; some were arrested and imprisoned. He read the attack as factional, a jab at the government that had chosen the site.
add_entries.source_note: Parenti, Storia fiorentina, under May 1504 (Matucci edition, later volume), as cited in the David literature; not checked against the edition here.

add_entries.headline: Letters from Florence: the ordeal fails, the friar is taken
add_entries.digest: Sanudo copied the reports that reached Venice of the failed fire ordeal and the storming of San Marco. In his diary the news sits among dispatches on the war over Pisa, where Venice backed Florence's rebels, and it reads as welcome trouble in a rival city.
add_entries.source_note: I diarii di Marin Sanudo, vol. 1 (ed. Stefani, 1879), entries for April 1498; exact day of arrival not checked.

add_entries.headline: Word comes that the friar has been burned
add_entries.digest: Within days, letters reported to Venice that Fra Girolamo and his two companions had been hanged and burned in the Piazza. Sanudo entered the news without comment of his own, as one item in a crowded run of dispatches.
add_entries.source_note: I diarii di Marin Sanudo, vol. 1, late May 1498; day of arrival not checked.

add_entries.headline: A Venetian paymaster's report of the raid on Montopoli
add_entries.digest: Sanudo copied into his diary a letter from Vincenzo Valier, a young Venetian paymaster with the troops defending Pisa against Florence. It describes a night march across the Arno, a dawn assault on the Florentine town of Montopoli, and the sack that followed. This is the war whose battles Florence would later commission Leonardo and Michelangelo to paint.
add_entries.source_note: Sanudo, I diarii, vol. 1, ed. F. Stefani (Venice, 1879), coll. 300–301; English translation at De Re Militari.

add_entries.headline: The marchioness asks what Leonardo is doing
add_entries.digest: Isabella wrote to Fra Pietro da Novellara in Florence. Her husband had given away the drawing Leonardo left at Mantua, so she wanted another sketch of her portrait; failing that, a small devotional Madonna. She asked the friar to find out what the painter was working on and how he lived.
add_entries.source_note: Isabella d'Este to Pietro da Novellara, Mantua, 27 March 1501, Archivio Gonzaga (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue).

add_entries.headline: A friar in the studio: St Anne, the lamb, and the assistants
add_entries.digest: Novellara reported that Leonardo's life was unsettled and that he was absorbed in mathematics. Two young assistants were painting portraits, and the master sometimes touched them up. The friar described a small cartoon in which the Christ Child slips from his mother's arms to seize a lamb while St Anne holds her back.
add_entries.source_note: Pietro da Novellara to Isabella d'Este, Florence, 3 April 1501, Archivio Gonzaga (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue).

add_entries.headline: A Madonna for the French king's secretary
add_entries.digest: On a second visit, Novellara found Leonardo friendly towards Isabella and willing to paint her once he had finished a small picture for Florimond Robertet, secretary to the King of France. He described it: the Virgin as if winding yarn, the Child holding the winder and gazing at its cross-shaped spokes. He added that geometry had made the painter impatient of the brush.
add_entries.source_note: Pietro da Novellara to Isabella d'Este, Florence, 14 April 1501, Archivio Gonzaga (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue).

add_entries.headline: A young Christ requested on the night the giant moves
add_entries.digest: Isabella wrote to Leonardo himself, recalling the charcoal portrait he had drawn at Mantua and his promise to make a coloured version. Since that seemed unlikely, she asked instead for a young Christ of about twelve. The same day she wrote to Angelo del Tovaglia in Florence asking him to press the painter. That evening, in Florence, the David began its journey from the Opera.
add_entries.source_note: Isabella d'Este to Leonardo and to Angelo del Tovaglia, Mantua, 14 May 1504, Archivio Gonzaga (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue).

add_entries.headline: Tovaglia's answer: the council's battle comes first
add_entries.digest: Angelo del Tovaglia reported from Florence that Leonardo had put off Isabella's commission because of the work for the Florentine government, the Battle of Anghiari, whose terms had been fixed only weeks earlier. The patron in Mantua learned what the city's own records show: the republic had claimed its painter.
add_entries.source_note: Angelo del Tovaglia to Isabella d'Este, Florence, 27 May 1504, Archivio Gonzaga (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue).

add_entries.headline: She writes to Leonardo again
add_entries.digest: Isabella wrote once more to Leonardo, still hoping for the picture while he was occupied with the Florentine battle painting. No painting from him ever reached her.
add_entries.source_note: Isabella d'Este to Leonardo, Mantua, 31 October 1504, Archivio Gonzaga (listed in the Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue; content summarised only in outline there).

add_convergences.label: The ordeal by fire
add_convergences.note: Landucci, a believer, saw a day of shame turned against the friar; Parenti, from the critics' side, saw his party beaten; in Venice Sanudo copied it all down as news of a rival in trouble.

add_convergences.label: A friar in Leonardo's studio
add_convergences.note: Isabella's questions from Mantua and Novellara's answers from Florence give a dated view of Leonardo between the Milan years and the Anghiari commission: a cartoon of St Anne, a Madonna for a Frenchman, and a painter who preferred geometry.

add_ties.note: Two Florentine chroniclers of the same days, the apothecary a follower of the friar and the patrician increasingly his critic.
Parenti followed the friar's career closely and with growing hostility, and recorded his fall as a political defeat.
She sent him to Leonardo with questions on 27 March 1501, and he answered on 3 and 14 April.
Leonardo drew her portrait in charcoal at Mantua in 1499–1500; her letter of 14 May 1504 reminds him of it and of his promise.

add_claims.claim: A cartoon of the Virgin, Child, St Anne and a lamb seen in Leonardo's studio
add_claims.evidence: Novellara to Isabella d'Este, 3 April 1501, Archivio di Stato di Mantova

add_claims.claim: Madonna of the Yarnwinder in progress for Florimond Robertet
add_claims.evidence: Novellara to Isabella d'Este, 14 April 1501, Archivio di Stato di Mantova

add_claims.claim: Isabella asks Leonardo for a young Christ of about twelve; deferred for Anghiari and never delivered
add_claims.evidence: Isabella to Leonardo, 14 May 1504; Tovaglia to Isabella, 27 May 1504; Archivio di Stato di Mantova

fix.note: Landucci watched with sorrow and recorded how many lost faith; Parenti, from the friar's critics, recorded it as the end of a political crisis; Sanudo in Venice copied the news among war dispatches; Commynes, in France, blamed the pope; within a month Machiavelli held office in the new regime; a year and a half later Botticelli's brother recorded a leading enemy's admission that no fault had been found.

updates.why: Adds the two new eyes whose entries fall on the execution; existing wording kept.
Isabella's letter to Leonardo is dated 14 May 1504 (Archivio di Stato di Mantova catalogue), the evening the giant left the Opera; Parenti records the stoning on the route.
